Legislative Update

Psi Upsilon has once again teamed up with more than 90 men's and women's Greek
organizations in support of the Collegiate Housing and Infrastructure Act of 2007 (H.R.643/
S.638) , currently pending in the U.S. House and Senate.

College fraternities and sororities are the largest private landlords for college students, housing
more than 250,000 men and women a year at no cost to the institutions. Passage of the Collegiate
1 lousing and Infrastructure Act would encourage new charitable contributions to improve life
safety systems and increase overall housing capacity for a growing student population.

Passage of this important legislation would amend the current Internal Revenue Code to
allow tax-deductible contributions made to fraternal foundations, such as The Psi Upsilon
Foundation , to be used for life safety and infrastructure improvements of Greek student
housing. These improvements could include updated lire detection and prevention systems
that would provide critical protection for students. Currently, such contributions may only be
used for exclusively educational purposes.

Thousands of Greek students and alumni , including hundreds of Psi Upsilon brothers,
have participated in a massive grassroots letter-writing campaign to members of Congress
seeking support for this legislation . In April , hundreds of Greek students and alumni leaders
held more than 300 meetings with members of Congress to seek additional support. These
efforts have resulted in 168 sponsors of the bill in the House and 34 in the Senate, a major
increase from the previous Congress.

BACKGROUND

• Under the current tax code, colleges and universities may expend tax-deductible charitable
contributions for the building, improvement or alteration of student facilities including
dormitories, dining halls, study areas, libraries, computers, laundry facilities, physical
fitness facilities and social or recreational areas.

• Conversely, fraternity and sorority educational foundations are allowed to expend tax-
deductible charitable contributions for the benefit of college students only if the grant is
of a purely educational nature, such as libraries, scholarships, leadership programming,
computer wiring and study facilities.

• There are many schools where the institution owns some, but not all. of the fraternity housing.
In those cases, the fraternal housing owned by the school enjoys the benefits of raising tax-
deductible funds for improvements while similarly situated students living in the other fraternity
housing cannot raise the tax-deductible funds needed to improve their own housing.

• The Collegiate Housing and Infrastructure Act eliminates the distinction between the
types of student facilities that may be provided by a tax-exempt college and those that may
-
be provided by another tax exempt charitable or educational organization to a collegiate
organization for the benefit of full- time college students. It allows fraternal education
foundations to have equivalent economic rights to fund collegiate housing as the universities
to build for similarly situated students.

• Fraternal educational foundations (501(c) (3) organizations would be able to make grants to
the not-for-profit house corporations of their respective undergraduate chapters (501 (c) (2) or
(c)(7) organizations for a larger array of purposes including bricks and mortar infrastructure
and life safety improvements to chapter housing.

IMPORTANT QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS

Is this change in the tax code creating preferential treatment for fraternities, sororities or
other organizations?

• The Act provides tax parity for all grants made to non-profit entities for the benefit of college
students. This legislative change would be the final step in leveling the playing field for
charitable giving to all organizations that provide non-profit housing, dining and educational
facilities that benefit college students.

• Other campus organizations, including some religiously affiliated and traditionally minority
organizations, will be able to use this change to fund their own expansion of grants for the
benefit of their student members.

• What the act really does is eliminate needless discrimination that favors one set of students
living in non -profit collegiate housing (owned by the host institutions) over similarly situated
students living in other non -profit collegiate housing (such as fraternity and
sorority housing) .

WHAT ARE THE PUBLIC BENEFITS OF FRATERNITY AND SORORITY HOUSING?

• Both public and private colleges and universities benefit from the presence of Greek housing.
• Greeks operate housing for more than 250,000 students at no cost to the host schools or the
American taxpayers. Greeks own and manage more than $3 billion in housing stock on college
campuses in the United States, but the replacement value of this housing is immeasurable.

• Most public universities and many private universities rely on Greek housing to support a
significant percentage of the school's student population.

• Most colleges/ universities are not equipped to handle the increased residential load caused by
the deterioration of Greek housing units, especially with the current spike in enrollment.

Success is a Science .. . and an Art
By Peter A . Howley, Delta '62 ( New York University )

Experience has taught me that launching a new business, especially a technology or
service product or service, starts with Science. My method involves looking for cold
hard facts combined with solid strategic thinking about these facts, followed later by
excellent detailed execution . Once successfully launched , the art of building a business
then becomes equally critical.

Working with new disruptive service and technology companies can be exciting work ,
offering experiences that rarely occur in large corporations. Unfortunately, many early
stage companies fail. So over the years I 've developed a general scientific approach for
analyzing the success potential and weighing the risks of a new business.

First , does the business make sense from the customers' viewpoint ? Many really
bright entrepreneurs have clever ideas, but are not good at synthesizing the related
PETER A HOWLEY, DELTA ' 62
business pieces involved. It 's critical to understand if the business idea truly meets a
customer need and to understand that need from the customer's perspective.

The second factor I look at is the entrepreneurs' plans for getting the product or
service to the customer. All too often unrealistic estimation takes place in determining
what it really takes to get a new product or service no matter how great the market .

The third critical factor I look for is competitive advantage. Perhaps the business idea
is great and the plans to get it to market are realistic. To be sustainable, a business
must have a competitive advantage.

The fourth step is to closely analyze the financials. Are the margins adequate, how
much capital and time is needed to reach breakeven and profitability? More important
are the financial assumptions themselves realistic?

My last checkpoint is evaluating the strength and experience of the management team .
A balanced starting team can be invaluable. Additional people can be brought in as
needed based on the company's growth .

The future of Psi Upsilon depends on loyal friends like Howard " Buzz" Webber.
Webber discovered the Phi chapter of Psi Upsilon in 1952 when he was a

Living in the Psi Upsilon house, pursuing bachelor's and master's degrees in

Sam Tinaglia, Omega ' 88

Sam credits Psi U for having a significant impact on his career. " I saw older brothers going
to Wall Street and saw a path I could follow," he said. In one instance a Psi U alumnus
sought him out, reviewed his resume and helped him get a job offer. Although he didn' t
pursue that job, his first job was on Wall Street and that initial offer helped pave the way.

Now a principal in a private investment bank , William Blair & Company, specializing in
mergers and acquisition. Tinaglia wants other brothers to have the opportunities he had . He
has found Wall Street jobs for four or live brothers and is always making Psi U connections.

One of his most revered and unexpected fraternity memories is of meeting Jay
Berwanger, Omega '3b and watching old black and white film reels of Berwanger playing
against Gerald Ford . Berwanger was the only Heisman recipient ever tackled by a future
president of the United States - during a 1934 game between Chicago and Michigan.

Sam enjoys his experience as a director and president-elect of The Psi Upsilon Foundation ,
which has allowed him to meet and work closely with other Psi U brothers on important
projects like the Order of the Owl (see page 53).

In June 2005, a group of alumni of the Zeta chapter at Dartmouth College
formed the Robert & Evelyn Kaiser Education Fund. Led by Errik Anderson

founding donors, all of them alumni brothers in the Zeta chapter. The founders

have been devoted chapter advisors for more than four decades.
